agents.name: claude
agents.description: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed.

agents.name: Explore
agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

agents.name: general-purpose
agents.description: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you.

agents.name: Plan
agents.description: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs.

agents.name: statusline-setup
agents.description: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting.

content.text:
This is outside the scope of software engineering work in this repo, but here's a solid explanation.

## Special Relativity (1905)

**Core postulates:**
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames.
2. The speed of light in vacuum (c ≈ 299,792,458 m/s) is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

**Key consequences:**

- **Time dilation**: A clock moving relative to an observer runs slower, by factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). At everyday speeds γ ≈ 1; near c, γ grows without bound. This is why GPS satellites need relativistic corrections — their clocks run faster than ground clocks due to weaker gravity, but slower due to orbital velocity, and both effects must be accounted for.

- **Length contraction**: An object moving relative to an observer appears contracted along its direction of motion by the same factor γ. A meter stick flying past you at high speed measures shorter than 1 meter, but from the stick's own frame, it's still 1 meter — it's you who appears contracted.

- **Relativity of simultaneity**: Events that are simultaneous in one reference frame are not necessarily simultaneous in another. There's no universal "now."

- **Mass-energy equivalence**: E = mc². Mass and energy are interchangeable; a small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy (this underlies nuclear fission/fusion).

- **Nothing with mass can reach c**: As velocity approaches c, relativistic momentum (and the energy needed to accelerate further) approaches infinity.

- **Spacetime**: Space and time are unified into a single 4-dimensional continuum. The spacetime interval between two events, s² = c²Δt² − Δx² − Δy² − Δz², is invariant — all observers agree on it even though they disagree on Δt and Δx individually.

## General Relativity (1915)

Extends special relativity to include gravity and acceleration.

**Core idea — the equivalence principle**: Being in a gravitational field is locally indistinguishable from being in an accelerating reference frame. There is no experiment you can do in a sealed box to tell whether you're sitting on Earth's surface or in a rocket accelerating at 9.8 m/s² in deep space.

**Gravity as curved spacetime**: Rather than treating gravity as a force (as Newton did), Einstein described it as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Massive objects warp the fabric of spacetime, and other objects (and light) follow the straightest possible paths (geodesics) through that curved geometry. As physicist John Wheeler summarized it: "Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve."

**The field equations**: Gµν = 8πG/c⁴ · Tµν — relates the curvature of spacetime (left side, the Einstein tensor) to the distribution of mass-energy (right side, the stress-energy tensor). These are ten coupled nonlinear differential equations, notoriously hard to solve except in symmetric cases (e.g., Schwarzschild's solution for a spherical mass).

**Key predictions, all experimentally confirmed:**

- **Gravitational time dilation**: Clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields. A clock at sea level ticks slightly slower than one on a mountaintop.
- **Gravitational lensing**: Light bends around massive objects, confirmed by Eddington's 1919 solar eclipse observation — the experiment that made Einstein famous.
- **Perihelion precession of Mercury**: GR correctly predicted the small extra precession of Mercury's orbit that Newtonian mechanics couldn't explain.
- **Gravitational redshift**: Light losing energy (shifting to longer wavelengths) as it climbs out of a gravity well.
- **Black holes**: Regions where spacetime curvature is so extreme that not even light can escape, bounded by an event horizon.
- **Gravitational waves**: Ripples in spacetime from accelerating massive objects (e.g., merging black holes), directly detected by LIGO in 2015, a century after prediction.
- **Frame dragging**: Rotating masses "drag" spacetime around with them, confirmed by Gravity Probe B.

## Why it matters practically

- GPS satellites must correct for both SR (velocity time dilation) and GR (gravitational time dilation) — without corrections, GPS would accumulate errors of about 10 km/day.
- It underpins modern cosmology (Big Bang theory, expansion of the universe, dark energy modeling).
- It predicts phenomena at the extremes: near black holes, at cosmological scales, and in high-precision timing systems.

Want me to go deeper on any specific part — the math of the field equations, the twin paradox, black hole thermodynamics, or how GR connects to (or conflicts with) quantum mechanics?
